title: Multi-region & failover math
description: Multi-region and failover reps for the disaster-recovery part of a system-design interview: how much acknowledged data a regional failover loses (RPO), the stages that make up the outage (RTO) and how many failovers a monthly budget affords, N+1 region capacity, the error budget one failover burns, the egress bill of a replication mesh, what chatty sequential round trips cost across regions (and the two ways out: a local replica or batching), hot-hot versus pilot-light standby cost, and the commit-throughput cap that cross-region consensus imposes. Every drill is whole-number arithmetic with the conversions named (per-mille = parts per thousand = x/1000; a 30-day billing month; money in integer cents), so you practise the reasoning, not the calculator.

exercises.title: Failover RPO: what the lag window loses
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The primary region takes 2,000 writes/s of 500 bytes each and replicates to the standby region asynchronously, running 30 seconds behind. The primary region dies. How much acknowledged data is gone?"

**Why it works.** With asynchronous cross-region replication a write is acknowledged before the other region has it. Everything acknowledged inside the lag window is lost when the primary region dies — that loss is the recovery point objective (RPO). Writes lost = writes per second × lag seconds; bytes lost = that × bytes per write. Synchronous replication drives the lag, and the RPO, to zero at the price of write latency.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `rpoEvents(writePerSec, lagSec)` → `writePerSec × lagSec`
- `rpoBytes(writePerSec, bytesPerWrite, lagSec)` → `writePerSec × bytesPerWrite × lagSec`

**Worked example.** 2,000 writes/s × 30 s of lag → **60,000** acknowledged writes lost.

tests.name: 2,000 writes/s x 30 s lag -> 60,000 lost writes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rpoEvents, 'function', 'export a function named rpoEvents');
assert.equal(mod.rpoEvents(2000, 30), 60000);

tests.name: synchronous replication -> nothing lost (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rpoEvents, 'function', 'export a function named rpoEvents');
assert.equal(mod.rpoEvents(2000, 0), 0);

tests.name: 150 writes/s x 600 s lag -> 90,000 lost writes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rpoEvents, 'function', 'export a function named rpoEvents');
assert.equal(mod.rpoEvents(150, 600), 90000);

tests.name: 2,000 writes/s x 500 B x 30 s -> 30,000,000 bytes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rpoBytes, 'function', 'export a function named rpoBytes');
assert.equal(mod.rpoBytes(2000, 500, 30), 30000000);

tests.name: 100 writes/s x 2,000 B x 5 s -> 1,000,000 bytes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rpoBytes, 'function', 'export a function named rpoBytes');
assert.equal(mod.rpoBytes(100, 2000, 5), 1000000);

tests.name: no writes in flight -> 0 bytes (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rpoBytes, 'function', 'export a function named rpoBytes');
assert.equal(mod.rpoBytes(0, 800, 120), 0);

exercises.explanation:
The replication lag is the data you agree to lose.

For `rpoBytes(2000, 500, 30)`:
- 2,000 writes/s × 500 bytes = 1,000,000 bytes/s
- × 30 s of lag = **30,000,000 bytes** (~30 MB) of acknowledged-but-unreplicated data gone

That is the RPO line in a DR plan — module 03's `staleWindowReads` counts the READS exposed in one lag window, while this counts the WRITES lost at failover.
hints: An async replica is always some seconds behind; ask what the primary acknowledged during those seconds that the standby never received.
events = writes/s × lagSec; bytes = writes/s × bytesPerWrite × lagSec.
Everything acknowledged inside the replication lag window is lost when the primary region dies: multiply writes per second by the lag seconds, and by bytes per write for the byte count

exercises.title: Failover RTO: detection, promotion, DNS
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Health checks fire every 5 s and we fail over after 3 missed beats; promoting the standby takes 45 s; clients cache DNS for 60 s. How long does each regional failover take — and how many of them fit in a 99.9% month?"

**Why it works.** A failover outage is a pipeline of stages that run in sequence: detection (heartbeat interval × missed beats before the region is declared dead), promotion of the standby, and the DNS TTL during which clients keep calling the old address. The month's downtime budget — about 43 minutes at 99.9%, about 4 minutes at 99.99% — converts to seconds (× 60); dividing by the per-failover RTO and rounding down gives how many failovers you can afford.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `rtoSeconds(heartbeatSec, missedBeats, promoteSec, dnsTtlSec)` → `heartbeatSec × missedBeats + promoteSec + dnsTtlSec`
- `failoversWithinBudget(budgetMinutesPerMonth, rtoSec)` → `Math.floor(budgetMinutesPerMonth × 60 ÷ rtoSec)`

**Worked example.** A 43-minute budget is 43 × 60 = 2,580 s; with 120 s failovers, 2,580 ÷ 120 = 21.5 → **21** failovers a month.

tests.name: 5 s beats x 3 missed + 45 s promote + 60 s TTL -> 120 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rtoSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named rtoSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.rtoSeconds(5, 3, 45, 60), 120);

tests.name: anycast / zero-TTL cutover -> 60 s (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rtoSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named rtoSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.rtoSeconds(5, 3, 45, 0), 60);

tests.name: 10 s beats x 6 missed + 120 s promote + 300 s TTL -> 480 s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.rtoSeconds, 'function', 'export a function named rtoSeconds');
assert.equal(mod.rtoSeconds(10, 6, 120, 300), 480);

tests.name: 43-minute budget with 120 s failovers -> 21
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.failoversWithinBudget, 'function', 'export a function named failoversWithinBudget');
assert.equal(mod.failoversWithinBudget(43, 120), 21);

tests.name: one 480 s failover already blows a 99.99% month -> 0 (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.failoversWithinBudget, 'function', 'export a function named failoversWithinBudget');
assert.equal(mod.failoversWithinBudget(4, 480), 0);

tests.name: 43-minute budget with 480 s failovers -> 5
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.failoversWithinBudget, 'function', 'export a function named failoversWithinBudget');
assert.equal(mod.failoversWithinBudget(43, 480), 5);

exercises.explanation:
RTO is the sum of the stages, and detection is derived, not given.

For `rtoSeconds(5, 3, 45, 60)`:
- detection: 5 s × 3 missed beats = 15 s
- promotion: 45 s
- DNS TTL: 60 s
- total: 15 + 45 + 60 = **120 s** per failover

43 minutes is 99.9%'s monthly budget — module 03's `error-budget` drill grants those minutes, and this failover pipeline spends them stage by stage.
hints: Walk the outage on a timeline: first nobody knows the region is dead, then the standby is being promoted, then clients still hold the old DNS answer.
RTO = heartbeat × missed + promote + TTL; failovers = ⌊budgetMin × 60 ÷ RTO⌋.

The outage is the sum of the stages: heartbeat × missed beats to detect, plus promotion, plus the DNS TTL clients keep caching — divide the month's downtime budget in seconds by that total and round down for how many failovers you can afford

exercises.title: N+1 regions: surviving the loss of one
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We serve 120,000 QPS spread evenly across 4 regions, and one region can carry 40,000 QPS. What does each survivor carry when a region dies — and how many regions do we need so that losing any one is a non-event?"

**Why it works.** When a region dies its share is redistributed over the survivors, so each one carries totalQps ÷ (regions − 1). The N+1 planning rule turns that around: deploy enough regions to carry the whole load at capacity, ⌈totalQps ÷ perRegionCapacityQps⌉, plus one spare so any single region can fail. `perRegionQpsAfterLoss` is only called with regions ≥ 2, and the tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `perRegionQpsAfterLoss(totalQps, regions)` → `totalQps ÷ (regions − 1)`
- `regionsToDeploy(totalQps, perRegionCapacityQps)` → `Math.ceil(totalQps ÷ perRegionCapacityQps) + 1`

**Worked example.** 120,000 QPS over 4 regions, one lost → 120,000 ÷ 3 = **40,000** QPS per survivor — exactly at capacity.

tests.name: 120,000 QPS over 4 regions, one lost -> 40,000 per survivor
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.perRegionQpsAfterLoss, 'function', 'export a function named perRegionQpsAfterLoss');
assert.equal(mod.perRegionQpsAfterLoss(120000, 4), 40000);

tests.name: lose one of two -> the survivor eats all 120,000 (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.perRegionQpsAfterLoss, 'function', 'export a function named perRegionQpsAfterLoss');
assert.equal(mod.perRegionQpsAfterLoss(120000, 2), 120000);

tests.name: 90,000 QPS over 3 regions, one lost -> 45,000 per survivor
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.perRegionQpsAfterLoss, 'function', 'export a function named perRegionQpsAfterLoss');
assert.equal(mod.perRegionQpsAfterLoss(90000, 3), 45000);

tests.name: 120,000 QPS at 40,000 per region -> 4, exact fit plus the spare (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.regionsToDeploy, 'function', 'export a function named regionsToDeploy');
assert.equal(mod.regionsToDeploy(120000, 40000), 4);

tests.name: 90,000 QPS at 40,000 per region -> 4 regions
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.regionsToDeploy, 'function', 'export a function named regionsToDeploy');
assert.equal(mod.regionsToDeploy(90000, 40000), 4);

tests.name: 30,000 QPS at 40,000 per region -> 2 regions
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.regionsToDeploy, 'function', 'export a function named regionsToDeploy');
assert.equal(mod.regionsToDeploy(30000, 40000), 2);

exercises.explanation:
Plan for the day one region is gone.

For `regionsToDeploy(120000, 40000)`:
- regions to carry the load: ⌈120,000 ÷ 40,000⌉ = 3
- plus one spare so any region can die → **4** regions (N+1)

With only 2 regions every region needs 100% headroom — module 07's `keysPerSurvivor` is the same survivor division for cache keys, and here it becomes the N+1 planning rule and a fleet size.
hints: Losing a region does not lose its traffic — the survivors absorb it, so size them for the day one is missing.
after loss = total ÷ (regions − 1); deploy = ⌈total ÷ capacity⌉ + 1.
After one region dies the survivors split the whole load, totalQps ÷ (regions − 1) — so deploy ceil(totalQps ÷ perRegionCapacity) regions for the load plus one spare for the failure

exercises.title: One failover, how much error budget
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A region serving 30,000 QPS goes dark for the 120 s our failover takes. The SLO allows 7,200,000 failed requests a month (roughly a 99.99% SLO on this traffic). How much of the month's error budget did that single incident burn?"

**Why it works.** During the RTO every request the dead region would have served fails, so one incident costs regionQps × rtoSec failed requests. Expressed against the month's allowed failures in per-mille (‰ = x/1000), it shows how many such incidents the SLO can survive. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `failedRequests(regionQps, rtoSec)` → `regionQps × rtoSec`
- `budgetBurnPermille(failedRequests, allowedFailuresPerMonth)` → `failedRequests × 1000 ÷ allowedFailuresPerMonth`

**Worked example.** 30,000 QPS dark for 120 s → **3,600,000** failed requests.

tests.name: 30,000 QPS dark for 120 s -> 3,600,000 failures
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.failedRequests, 'function', 'export a function named failedRequests');
assert.equal(mod.failedRequests(30000, 120), 3600000);

tests.name: instant failover -> 0 failures (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.failedRequests, 'function', 'export a function named failedRequests');
assert.equal(mod.failedRequests(30000, 0), 0);

tests.name: 5,000 QPS dark for 480 s -> 2,400,000 failures
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.failedRequests, 'function', 'export a function named failedRequests');
assert.equal(mod.failedRequests(5000, 480), 2400000);

tests.name: 3,600,000 of 7,200,000 allowed -> 500 permille
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetBurnPermille, 'function', 'export a function named budgetBurnPermille');
assert.equal(mod.budgetBurnPermille(3600000, 7200000), 500);

tests.name: the whole month's budget in one incident -> 1000 permille (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetBurnPermille, 'function', 'export a function named budgetBurnPermille');
assert.equal(mod.budgetBurnPermille(2400000, 2400000), 1000);

tests.name: 90,000 of 9,000,000 allowed -> 10 permille
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetBurnPermille, 'function', 'export a function named budgetBurnPermille');
assert.equal(mod.budgetBurnPermille(90000, 9000000), 10);

exercises.explanation:
An incident's cost is its traffic times its duration.

For `budgetBurnPermille(3600000, 7200000)`:
- a 120 s outage at 30,000 QPS fails 3,600,000 requests
- 3,600,000 × 1000 ÷ 7,200,000 = **500‰**

At a roughly 99.99% SLO half the month's error budget goes in one 120 s failover (12/02's RTO); at 12/02's 99.9% the same outage would cost about 46‰ — module 04's `latency-slo-budget` is a daily slow-request allowance, while this is a single incident's bite out of the monthly failure allowance.
hints: While the failover runs, the traffic aimed at the dead region has nowhere to go — count it.
failed = regionQps × rtoSec; burn‰ = failed × 1000 ÷ allowedPerMonth.
Every request the dead region would have served during the RTO fails, regionQps × rtoSec — scale by 1000 ÷ the month's allowed failures to see the budget share one incident burns

exercises.title: Replication mesh: the cross-region egress bill
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The application writes 200 GB a day in total; each write lands in its home region and is replicated to every other region. We run 4 regions and cross-region transfer costs 2¢ per GB. What is the monthly replication bill, and what does adding a fifth region do to it?"

**Why it works.** In an all-to-all mesh every write leaves its home region once per peer, so daily replication egress is writeGbPerDay × (regions − 1). The bill uses a 30-day billing month and money in integer cents. Every region you add re-bills the whole write stream one more time.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `meshEgressGbPerDay(writeGbPerDay, regions)` → `writeGbPerDay × (regions − 1)`
- `meshMonthlyCents(writeGbPerDay, regions, centsPerGb)` → `writeGbPerDay × (regions − 1) × 30 × centsPerGb`

**Worked example.** 200 GB/day across 4 regions → 200 × 3 = **600 GB** of replication egress a day.

tests.name: 200 GB/day across 4 regions -> 600 GB/day
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.meshEgressGbPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named meshEgressGbPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.meshEgressGbPerDay(200, 4), 600);

tests.name: single region -> no replication egress (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.meshEgressGbPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named meshEgressGbPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.meshEgressGbPerDay(200, 1), 0);

tests.name: 50 GB/day across 3 regions -> 100 GB/day
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.meshEgressGbPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named meshEgressGbPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.meshEgressGbPerDay(50, 3), 100);

tests.name: 200 GB/day, 4 regions, 2 cents/GB -> 36,000 cents/month
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.meshMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named meshMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.meshMonthlyCents(200, 4, 2), 36000);

tests.name: 50 GB/day, 3 regions, 9 cents/GB -> 27,000 cents/month
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.meshMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named meshMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.meshMonthlyCents(50, 3, 9), 27000);

tests.name: 1,000 GB/day, 2 regions, 2 cents/GB -> 60,000 cents/month
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.meshMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named meshMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.meshMonthlyCents(1000, 2, 2), 60000);

exercises.explanation:
Regions − 1 multiplies the write stream itself.

For `meshMonthlyCents(200, 4, 2)`:
- daily egress: 200 GB × 3 peers = 600 GB
- monthly: 600 × 30 = 18,000 GB
- bill: 18,000 × 2¢ = **36,000¢** ($360/month)
- a fifth region: 200 × 4 × 30 × 2 = 48,000¢, another 12,000¢ for the same writes

Every region you add re-bills the whole write stream — module 10's `monthlyBillCents` prices USER-facing egress, while this is the internal mesh where the region count multiplies the writes.
hints: A write is born in one region and must reach every other one — count how many times it crosses a region boundary.
egress/day = writeGb × (regions − 1); cents/month = writeGb × (regions − 1) × 30 × centsPerGb.
Every write leaves its home region once per peer, writeGb × (regions − 1) per day — multiply by 30 days and the per-GB cents for the monthly replication bill

exercises.title: Hot-hot vs pilot light: what DR costs
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "One region of our stack costs $4,000 a month. Running hot-hot in two regions doubles that. A pilot-light standby keeps the second region 10% warm and scales it up only during a disaster. What does each DR topology cost per month?"

**Why it works.** Hot-hot (active-active) pays the full regional price in every region. Pilot light pays one full region plus a warm per-mille slice of a second (‰ = x/1000) — data replicated and a skeleton fleet running. Money is in integer cents: $4,000 = 400,000¢. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `hotHotMonthlyCents(perRegionCents, regions)` → `perRegionCents × regions`
- `pilotLightMonthlyCents(perRegionCents, warmPermille)` → `perRegionCents + perRegionCents × warmPermille ÷ 1000`

**Worked example.** 400,000¢ per region × 2 regions → **800,000¢** a month hot-hot.

tests.name: 400,000 cents x 2 regions -> 800,000 cents hot-hot
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.hotHotMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named hotHotMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.hotHotMonthlyCents(400000, 2), 800000);

tests.name: one region -> no DR at all, 400,000 cents (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.hotHotMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named hotHotMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.hotHotMonthlyCents(400000, 1), 400000);

tests.name: 250,000 cents x 3 regions -> 750,000 cents
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.hotHotMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named hotHotMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.hotHotMonthlyCents(250000, 3), 750000);

tests.name: pilot light at 100 permille warm -> 440,000 cents
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pilotLightMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named pilotLightMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.pilotLightMonthlyCents(400000, 100), 440000);

tests.name: fully warm standby -> the hot-hot price, 800,000 cents (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pilotLightMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named pilotLightMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.pilotLightMonthlyCents(400000, 1000), 800000);

tests.name: 250,000 cents at 200 permille warm -> 300,000 cents
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pilotLightMonthlyCents, 'function', 'export a function named pilotLightMonthlyCents');
assert.equal(mod.pilotLightMonthlyCents(250000, 200), 300000);

exercises.explanation:
The standby's warmth is the dial between cost and recovery time.

For `pilotLightMonthlyCents(400000, 100)`:
- primary region: 400,000¢
- standby at 100‰ warm: 400,000 × 100 ÷ 1000 = 40,000¢
- total: **440,000¢** against 800,000¢ hot-hot

Pilot light saves 45% and pays for it in RTO, because the standby must scale up mid-outage (12/02) — module 01's `cost-per-month` bills one fleet, while this compares DR topologies.
hints: Hot-hot runs two full copies all the time; pilot light keeps the second copy mostly switched off until it is needed.
hotHot = perRegion × regions; pilotLight = perRegion + perRegion × warm‰ ÷ 1000.
Hot-hot pays the full region price times the region count — pilot light pays one full region plus the warm per-mille slice of a second, per × warm‰ ÷ 1000 added on

exercises.title: Cross-region consensus: the speed-of-light cap
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our globally consistent database runs consensus across regions 100 ms apart, and every commit needs one quorum round. How many commits per second can it do one at a time — and with group commit packing 500 commits into each round?"

**Why it works.** If each commit needs its own consensus round and rounds run one after another, the inter-region round trip behaves like a critical section: at most 1000 ÷ rttMs rounds fit in a second (1 s = 1,000 ms). This is module 06's lock-serialization math with the WAN round trip as the hold time — and module 06's batching lesson is the escape hatch: pack commitsPerRound commits into every round and the cap multiplies by the batch size. The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `consensusCommitsPerSec(interRegionRttMs)` → `1000 ÷ interRegionRttMs`
- `batchedCommitsPerSec(interRegionRttMs, commitsPerRound)` → `commitsPerRound × 1000 ÷ interRegionRttMs`

**Worked example.** A 100 ms inter-region RTT → 1000 ÷ 100 = **10** commits/s, one round at a time.

tests.name: 100 ms RTT -> 10 commits/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.consensusCommitsPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named consensusCommitsPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.consensusCommitsPerSec(100), 10);

tests.name: a 1-second RTT -> one round per second (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.consensusCommitsPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named consensusCommitsPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.consensusCommitsPerSec(1000), 1);

tests.name: 8 ms RTT -> 125 commits/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.consensusCommitsPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named consensusCommitsPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.consensusCommitsPerSec(8), 125);

tests.name: 100 ms RTT, 500 commits per round -> 5,000 commits/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedCommitsPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named batchedCommitsPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.batchedCommitsPerSec(100, 500), 5000);

tests.name: unbatched = the raw cap, 10 commits/s (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedCommitsPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named batchedCommitsPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.batchedCommitsPerSec(100, 1), 10);

tests.name: 40 ms RTT, 200 commits per round -> 5,000 commits/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedCommitsPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named batchedCommitsPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.batchedCommitsPerSec(40, 200), 5000);

exercises.explanation:
The round trip caps the rounds; the batch multiplies what each round carries.

For `batchedCommitsPerSec(100, 500)`:
- one quorum round costs 100 ms → 1000 ÷ 100 = 10 rounds/s
- 500 commits share each round → 10 × 500 = **5,000 commits/s**

Group commit is how global databases survive the speed of light — a declared re-skin of module 06's `lock-serialization` (the same 1000 ÷ ms for a local critical section), extended with 06's batching so the WAN round trip is amortized.
hints: If rounds cannot overlap, the round trip is a lock you hold — ask how many such holds fit in one second.
rounds/s = 1000 ÷ rttMs; batched = commitsPerRound × 1000 ÷ rttMs.
Each consensus round costs one inter-region RTT, so sequential rounds cap at 1000 ÷ rttMs per second — packing commitsPerRound into every round multiplies that cap by the batch size

exercises.title: Chatty pages across regions: the round trips add up
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our EU web tier renders a page with 12 sequential database queries against the primary in the US, 180 ms away. An in-region replica would answer in 20 ms. What does the page spend on the network today — and could we win the same without a replica by batching the queries?"

**Why it works.** A query that needs the previous answer cannot start until that answer is back, so sequential queries pay the round-trip time one after another: the network cost of the page is the RTT times the number of sequential round trips. That leaves two levers. A local replica shrinks the RTT. Batching (one query that fetches what several did, or several statements per round trip) shrinks the number of trips: queries ÷ queries-per-trip, rounded up, because a partly filled trip still costs a full round trip.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `pageNetworkMs(rttMs, sequentialRoundTrips)` → the time the page spends waiting on the network
- `batchedPageMs(rttMs, queries, queriesPerRoundTrip)` → the same wait once the queries are packed into round trips of `queriesPerRoundTrip`

**Worked example.** 12 sequential queries at a 180 ms RTT → 12 × 180 = **2,160 ms** of network wait for one page.

tests.name: 12 sequential queries at 180 ms -> 2,160 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pageNetworkMs, 'function', 'export a function named pageNetworkMs');
assert.equal(mod.pageNetworkMs(180, 12), 2160);

tests.name: the same 12 queries against a 20 ms local replica -> 240 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pageNetworkMs, 'function', 'export a function named pageNetworkMs');
assert.equal(mod.pageNetworkMs(20, 12), 240);

tests.name: a single query -> one round trip, 180 ms (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pageNetworkMs, 'function', 'export a function named pageNetworkMs');
assert.equal(mod.pageNetworkMs(180, 1), 180);

tests.name: 12 queries batched 6 per trip -> 2 trips, 360 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedPageMs, 'function', 'export a function named batchedPageMs');
assert.equal(mod.batchedPageMs(180, 12, 6), 360);

tests.name: 12 queries batched 5 per trip -> 3 trips, 540 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedPageMs, 'function', 'export a function named batchedPageMs');
assert.equal(mod.batchedPageMs(180, 12, 5), 540);

tests.name: one query per trip -> no batching, 2,160 ms (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedPageMs, 'function', 'export a function named batchedPageMs');
assert.equal(mod.batchedPageMs(180, 12, 1), 2160);

tests.name: all 12 in one trip -> 180 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.batchedPageMs, 'function', 'export a function named batchedPageMs');
assert.equal(mod.batchedPageMs(180, 12, 12), 180);

exercises.explanation:
Distance is paid per round trip, not per page.

For `batchedPageMs(180, 12, 5)`:
- 12 queries at 5 per round trip → ⌈12 ÷ 5⌉ = 3 trips (the last one is only partly full)
- 3 × 180 ms = **540 ms**, against 2,160 ms sent one by one

The in-region replica (12 × 20 = 240 ms) and batching into 2 trips (360 ms) land in the same range, and batching needs no new database — fix the N+1 query pattern before you buy geo-replication.
